source.name: ASTRA Bio wave 1 — Breathing and Respiration
source.license: Original syllabus-based practice questions (exam-frequent themes; not verbatim past papers)

questions.stem: The volume of air inspired or expired during a normal quiet breath is called
questions.explanation: Tidal volume is about 500 mL in a healthy adult at rest.

questions.stem: Nearly 97 percent of oxygen is carried from the lungs to tissues as
questions.explanation: Most O2 binds iron of haemoglobin; only about 3 percent travels dissolved in plasma.

questions.stem: The major form in which carbon dioxide is transported in human blood is
questions.explanation: About 70 percent of CO2 travels as HCO3-; the rest is carbamino-Hb or dissolved gas.

questions.stem: The actual sites of exchange of O2 and CO2 in the lungs are the
questions.explanation: Alveoli provide a thin, moist, highly vascular surface for diffusion of respiratory gases.

questions.stem: During quiet inspiration the diaphragm
questions.explanation: Contraction flattens the diaphragm, increasing thoracic volume so air flows in.

questions.stem: Oxygen diffuses from alveolar air into pulmonary capillary blood because alveolar pO2 is
questions.explanation: Alveolar pO2 is about 104 mm Hg versus about 40 mm Hg in deoxygenated blood, so O2 enters the capillary.

questions.stem: The basic respiratory rhythm centre of humans is located in the
questions.explanation: The medullary rhythm centre sets the breathing rate; the pons modulates it.

questions.stem: Inflammation that narrows bronchioles and causes wheezing attacks is typical of
questions.explanation: Asthma is reversible bronchoconstriction with mucus; emphysema destroys alveolar walls.

questions.stem: The respiratory quotient (CO2 released / O2 used) for a pure carbohydrate diet is
questions.explanation: Oxidation of glucose yields equal moles of CO2 and O2 consumed, so RQ = 1.

questions.stem: A rise in blood pCO2 and H+ concentration shifts the oxyhaemoglobin curve to the
options: right and favours unloading of O2
right and prevents any O2 release
questions.explanation: This Bohr effect helps haemoglobin give up oxygen in active tissues.

questions.stem: Vital capacity of the lungs is the sum of
questions.explanation: VC is the maximum air that can be expired after a deepest inspiration: TV + IRV + ERV.

questions.stem: Each haemoglobin molecule can bind a maximum of how many molecules of oxygen?
questions.explanation: Hb has four haem groups, so it carries up to four O2 molecules (Hb4O8).

questions.stem: When HCO3- leaves a red cell in a tissue capillary, electroneutrality is kept by entry of Cl- (Hamburger phenomenon). This chloride shift is reversed in the
questions.explanation: In the lung, HCO3- re-enters RBCs, Cl- leaves, and CO2 is exhaled.

questions.stem: Residual volume is the air that
options: is exchanged in one quiet breath
remains in the lungs after a forceful expiration
can still be inspired after a normal inspiration
fills only the anatomical dead space
questions.explanation: About 1100–1200 mL stays after maximal expiration and cannot be expelled voluntarily.

questions.stem: Binding of the first O2 molecule to haemoglobin
options: raises affinity for the next O2 molecules
questions.explanation: Cooperative binding gives the sigmoid O2-dissociation curve of haemoglobin.

questions.stem: Carbonic anhydrase, which speeds formation of carbonic acid from CO2 and water, is abundant in
questions.explanation: RBCs contain carbonic anhydrase; plasma has very little, so most HCO3- forms inside red cells.

questions.stem: Which structure is shared by the respiratory and digestive pathways?
questions.explanation: The pharynx is a common passage; the epiglottis then directs food away from the larynx.

questions.stem: Quiet expiration in a healthy person is mainly
options: an active process driven by abdominal muscles
a passive elastic recoil of lungs and chest wall
caused by contraction of the external intercostals
produced by flattening of the diaphragm
questions.explanation: After inspiration, stretched lungs and raised diaphragm recoil; forced expiration needs internal intercostals and abdomen.

questions.stem: pCO2 is highest in which of the following?
questions.explanation: Tissues produce CO2, so venous/tissue-capillary pCO2 (about 45 mm Hg) exceeds alveolar pCO2 (40 mm Hg).

questions.stem: The pneumotaxic centre in the pons mainly
options: starts inspiration and never stops it
detects only arterial O2 in the aorta
questions.explanation: Pneumotaxic signals switch off inspiration, thereby moderating tidal volume and rate.

questions.stem: Destruction of alveolar walls, often linked to cigarette smoking, characterises
questions.explanation: Emphysema reduces surface area for gas exchange; asthma is bronchoconstriction.

questions.stem: A respiratory quotient close to 0.7 indicates that the substrate being oxidised is mainly
questions.explanation: Fats need more O2 per CO2 formed, so RQ is about 0.7; protein is about 0.9.

questions.stem: Which change does not favour unloading of oxygen from haemoglobin?
questions.explanation: Higher pH (Bohr reverse) increases O2 affinity; heat, CO2, H+ and 2,3-BPG decrease it.

questions.stem: Functional residual capacity (FRC) equals
questions.explanation: FRC is the air left after a normal expiration: expiratory reserve plus residual volume.

questions.stem: Which statement about oxygen transport is incorrect?
options: A fully saturated Hb molecule carries four O2
Myoglobin shows a hyperbolic dissociation curve
Most O2 in arterial blood is dissolved, not bound to Hb
Low tissue pO2 promotes O2 release from Hb
questions.explanation: Only about 3 percent of O2 is dissolved; the rest is oxyhaemoglobin.

questions.stem: Identify the incorrect statement about CO2 carriage.
options: About 20–25 percent of CO2 binds Hb as carbamino-haemoglobin
Carbonic anhydrase is required for rapid HCO3- formation in RBCs
Chloride ions enter RBCs in tissues as HCO3- leaves them
Nearly all CO2 travels as dissolved gas in plasma
questions.explanation: Dissolved CO2 is only about 7 percent; bicarbonate is the main transport form.
